qs.q: A 3-day-old term male infant presents with failure to pass meconium, bilious vomiting, and progressive abdominal distension. Digital rectal examination reveals a tight, empty rectum, followed by an explosive passage of stool and flatus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: The clinical presentation of delayed meconium passage, abdominal distension, and the 'squirt sign' following digital rectal examination with an empty rectum is classic for Hirschsprung disease. Meconium ileus typically presents with a patent, normal-toned anus and is associated with cystic fibrosis.

qs.q: A surgeon is performing a definitive pull-through procedure for Hirschsprung disease where the aganglionic rectum is excised down to about 2 cm above the dentate line, followed by an end-to-end anastomosis. Which specific operation does this describe?
qs.e: The Swenson operation involves excising the aganglionic rectum down to 2 cm above the dentate line and performing a direct end-to-end anastomosis. The Duhamel and Soave procedures utilize different techniques for managing the rectal wall and cuff.

qs.q: During a Duhamel pull-through procedure for Hirschsprung disease, the rectum is left in place and oversewn, while the normal bowel is brought down through a specific retrorectal space and anastomosed above the dentate line. Where is this normal bowel brought down?
o: Anterior to the bladder and prostate
Lateral to the levator ani muscles
qs.e: In the Duhamel procedure, the normal bowel is brought down behind the rectum, specifically in the space between the sacrum and the rectum. The Soave procedure involves pulling the bowel through a mucosal muscular cuff instead.

qs.q: During the planning of a Soave endorectal pull-through, the surgical technique relies on a specific plane of dissection within the rectum. What is dissected away from the muscular cuff?
qs.e: In the Soave endorectal pull-through, the mucosa is dissected from the muscular cuff before the normal bowel is pulled through. Dissecting the serosa or mesorectal fat would violate the correct endorectal surgical plane.

qs.q: A 9-month-old infant presents with vomiting and the passage of blood and mucus per rectum, commonly described as redcurrant jelly stool. What is the primary pathophysiological cause of this specific stool finding?
o: Necrosis of a Meckel's diverticulum acting as a lead point
Bacterial enterotoxin production by invading rotavirus strains
Rapid transit of bile salts mixed with upper gastrointestinal blood
Mucosal shedding and hemorrhage from congested, ischaemic mucosa
qs.e: Redcurrant jelly stool consists of mucus and blood resulting from the congested and ischaemic mucosa as the trapped mesentery undergoes venous compression. It is typically a late sign appearing 12 to 24 hours after the onset of symptoms.

qs.q: A 63-year-old woman presents with alternating constipation and diarrhoea, tenesmus, and passage of stool mixed with mucus and bright red blood. A digital rectal examination is performed. What is the most likely physical finding expected on examination of the rectum?
qs.e: Digital rectal examination of a rectal cancer typically reveals a hard, ulcerated mass that may be mobile or fixed. Soft compressible swellings are characteristic of haemorrhoids rather than malignant ulcers.
qs.s: Colorectal Cancer: Presentation, Staging and Surgical Management: MCQs

qs.q: Following initial venous drainage from the colon and rectum, where do colorectal cancer metastases typically spread first via the haematogenous route?
qs.e: Haematogenous spread from the colorectum travels via the portal venous system to the liver first, before secondary dissemination to the lungs and bone. Low rectal tumours can occasionally bypass the portal system to drain directly to the lungs.
qs.s: Colorectal Cancer: Presentation, Staging and Surgical Management: MCQs

qs.q: A 72-year-old institutionalized man with Parkinson disease presents with rapid, massive abdominal distension, absolute constipation, and acute colicky lower abdominal pain. His abdomen is tense, tympanitic, and drum-like with an empty rectum on digital examination. There is no rebound tenderness or guarding. What is the most common underlying predisposing factor for this condition in African hospi
o: Prior abdominal surgery and peritoneal adhesions
Malignant stricture of the descending colon
A high-fibre diet with a long redundant sigmoid
Congenital aganglionic megacolon of the rectum
qs.e: Sigmoid volvulus is commonly predisposed to by a high-fibre diet leading to a bulky stool load and a long redundant sigmoid colon with a narrow-based mesentery. In African hospitals, it accounts for over 50% of intestinal obstructions, unlike Western nations where cancer is more frequent.
qs.s: Sigmoid and Caecal Volvulus: Diagnosis and Management: MCQs

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The rectum is the final 12‑15 cm of the large intestine, storing feces before evacuation. Its anatomy determines the presentation of bleeding, pain, and obstruction.

sections.p: The rectum continues the sigmoid colon and ends at the anorectal junction, where the internal anal sphincter begins.
b: Length ≈ 12‑15 cm
Divided into three zones: upper, middle, lower

sections.p: It lies in the pelvis, anterior to the sacrum and coccyx, posterior to the prostate/uterus, and is covered by the mesorectum.
b: Mucosa: columnar epithelium with goblet cells
Submucosa contains hemorrhoidal vascular plexus
Muscularis: inner circular, outer longitudinal

sections.p: Anteriorly it contacts the bladder (men) or uterus (women); laterally the levator ani and piriformis; posteriorly the sacrum and coccyx.
b: Important for surgical planes
Tumor spread follows these fascial planes

sections.p: Arterial supply comes from the superior rectal artery (branch of IMA) and the middle/lower rectal arteries (branches of internal iliac). Venous drainage mirrors arteries to portal and systemic systems.
b: Superior rectal → portal system (risk of portal hypertension varices)
Middle/lower rectal → systemic (risk of hemorrhoids)

sections.p: Parasympathetic innervation via pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2‑S4) stimulates motility; sympathetic fibers (L1‑L2) control sphincter tone. Sensory afferents convey pain from the upper two‑thirds (visceral) and lower third (somatic).
b: Visceral pain is vague, referred to lower back
Somatic pain is sharp, perianal

sections.p: Stores feces, coordinates defecation via reflexes (gastrocolic, recto‑anal), and maintains continence through internal/external sphincters.
b: Recto‑anal inhibitory reflex relaxes internal sphincter when rectum distends
External sphincter under voluntary control

sections.p: Rectal pathology often presents with bleeding, pain, or altered bowel habits. Understanding anatomy guides examination, imaging, and surgery.
b: Rectal cancer: arises from mucosa, spreads along mesorectal fascia
Hemorrhoids: dilation of superior/inferior rectal plexus
Fistula-in-ano: tracks through intersphincteric space
Trauma: can perforate posterior wall against sacrum

t.b: Detects masses, tone, fissures; a firm, irregular mass suggests cancer
Visualizes mucosa; ulcerative colitis shows continuous erythema from rectum
Staging rectal cancer; assesses mesorectal involvement, sphincter invasion

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams and bedside assessment.
b: Rectal bleeding without upper GI signs points to colorectal source.
An empty rectum with a gush of stool on withdrawal suggests Hirschsprung disease in infants.
Continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum is characteristic of ulcerative colitis.

whenToSeekHelp: Profuse rectal bleeding causing hemodynamic instability
Sudden severe abdominal pain with peritoneal signs (possible perforation)
Unexplained weight loss with persistent change in bowel habit

faq.q: Why is rectal bleeding often painless in ulcerative colitis?
faq.a: Inflammation is limited to the mucosa, sparing deeper pain fibers.

faq.q: What distinguishes a hemorrhoid from a rectal tumor on exam?
faq.a: Hemorrhoids are compressible vascular cushions; tumors are firm, fixed, and may ulcerate.

faq.q: When is a colonoscopy preferred over sigmoidoscopy?
faq.a: When the disease may extend beyond the rectosigmoid or when full colonic assessment is needed.
